title: Simulations not identical with tree is initialized on different cells
body:
When the tree is initialized in different locations across an identical scene (with toric symmetry ON in all direction), the simulations should all be identical - especially tree growth. 

@kevinwolz & @LECOMTE-ISADEV worked on this for a long time and found (and fixed!) several bugs so far that were collectively leading to this issue:

- When the intercrop area extended beyond the edge of the scene, it was not being initialized on the other side of the scene via toric symmetry.

- When calculating root growth and C allocation, the distance from the root to the tree is critical. The distance was not being calculated correctly when roots stretch across toric symmetry to the other side of the scene.

- Rounding errors on root growth variables, as a result of voxels being calculated in different orders when the tree is in different places.

**However, the simulations are still not completely identical.** It seems that the first differences are small differences that appear in N content in the soil. They start small, but the simulations really diverge over time. Overall, the effect is now quite minor compared to when we first noticed this, but there still should be no reason why this is happening. Further investigation is necessary into why these differences are occurring.

title: Tree roots should be able to colonize same voxel twice around toric symmetry
body:
Currently in Hi-sAFe, a given tree’s roots can only enter and colonize a voxel ONE time (i.e. from one parent coarse root). As confirmed by @LECOMTE-ISADEV on 20 Feb 2018, this is true even if the second root is coming from "around" toric symmetry. 

However, it can be argued that, if a root is coming from "around" toric symmetry, this root is theoretically from a DIFFERENT tree. It should, therefore, be allowed to colonize the same voxel as the original tree. 

It is unclear how much of an impact this would have on the simulation/tree growth since any water/nitrogen extracted by this second root is going to go to the same, original tree anyway. What would be different, though, is the distance those resources have to travel. SO, the impact is likely small, but fixing this could still impact tree root architecture over the long term, especially in simulations where tree density is high.

title: Better solution for "reportWaterCrop" and "reportWaterTree" errors

Sometimes the model prints out the message “Cell XX reportWaterCrop = X.XXXXX” or “Cell XX reportWaterTree = X.XXXXX”. 

@LECOMTE-ISADEV says that this message gets printed when a test is failed during the process of converting voxel water content to minicouche water content. For each minicouche, it checks if the water content is reasonable (e.g. not above field capacity) before saving the value. If it is not, then excess water is passed to the next minicouche, and so on. If there still excess at the end, then the excess disappears and this report message is printed. It seems very rare and pertains to very small values, but **there should be a better way to deal with this.**

title: Implement tree-tree canopy interactions
body:
There is NO algorithm in Hi-sAFe for tree-tree canopy interactions. Currently, this only works if tree spacing is the same as plotWidth and plotHeight (i.e. there is only a single tree on the scene and toric symmetry is on in all directions). For example, if you put two identical trees on the scene, both will grow to the dimensions of plotWidth and plotHeight, even if that means overlapping canopies.

Many theoretical questions need to be answered about how the trees "should" react before this is implemented in the code. For example, if there is one tall tree and one short tree, and their canopies are in two totally different levels, can the short tree grow horizontally underneath the taller tree canopy? If so, what happens if that short tree then begins to grow taller and runs into the tall tree? Is it forced to stay short? Does it grow around the tall tree somehow? Or should it not have been allowed to grow under the tall tree in the first place!?

title: Carbon allocation module hyper-sensitive to branch pruning during growing season
body:
The carbon allocation module is extremely sensitive to branch pruning events that occur in the middle of the growing season. After branch pruning, ALL carbon is allocated aboveground until the branch pool returns to equilibrium. Christian says that this is not realistic because the trees really don’t attempt to replenish the branch biomass until the following year. Fixing this will require a modification to the carbon allocation module that limits carbon allocation to branches to either (1) a limited amount each day (analogous to what is done for flux out of the NSC pool) and/or (2) a switch that modifies allocation to branches during certain phenological periods or after a pruning event. (solid vertical lines is transition from phenological stage 1 to 2; dashed vertical lines are branch pruning)

title: Enhance treeDensityReduction module
body:
The new branch pruning formalism that includes the **treeDensityReduction** parameter is too simplistic. It reduces the branch biomass, leaf biomass, and leaf area, but it does not induce the following proceses, which would be more accurate. For Daniel’s project, @kevinwolz manually adjusted **woodAreaDensity** and **clumpingCoef** since we were only running for one year anyone and could assume this steady state. 

Even though, the “branch density” of the crown has been reduced by **treeDensityReduction**% (because the crown volume stays the same while leaf and branch biomass are reduced), this does not change the light interception by the branches, as this is controlled by a fixed tree parameter (**woodAreaDensity**). 

When leaf growth occurs in the spring on a tree with the “full density” of branches and a tree with “half density” of branches, the time to reach the target leafArea is essentially the same. This occurs despite the fact that, in reality, a tree with fewer branches is likely going to take longer to reach the same leafArea. Perhaps some formalism can be added that scales leaf growth based on branch density “satisfaction”. Otherwise, if one thinks that these two trees will truly reach the target leafArea at the same rate, then the leaf clumpiness (**clumpingCoef**) must be changed to reflect that the leaves on the “half density” tree are certainly going to be more clumped. Perhaps leaf clumpiness can be proportional to a ratio between “branch density” and “target branch density”.

title: Rebuild the method of specifying Hi-sAFe outputs
body:
There are several aspects of the current approach to specifying outputs that are very inefficient. Collectively, I think these warrant a complete rebuild of the output specification system, rather than incremental improvements. **Lots of discussion necessary before starting on this one!**

- The variables.txt and subjects.txt approach to output variable definition/coding is very inefficient and sensitive to many issues. We need a different approach. These two files should not be necessary at all! I don't know exactly they're used within Hi-sAFe, but they really don't provide any information that cannot be gleaned from the name of variables in the .PRO file and, perhaps, a header that specifics which object the data is coming from (e.g. cells, plots, etc.)

- Having to repeat "SafePlot-", "SafeCell-", etc. before each output variable in the .PRO file is unnecessary. Can't this just be added as a single header that the output script reads and knows?

- Having all of the variables in the .PRO files listed on one line is a nightmare! Can't we instead have /n be the separator (e.g. between a header tag and ending tag)?

- Having a separate .PRO for each object type has its pros and cons. Another method would be to just have all of the output variables in one text file (maybe still separated into sections), and then each one has a numerical parameter net to it indicated how often it will get written out (e.g. 1 for daily, 30 for monthly, 365 for annually). I’m simplifying it a bit here, but in general I think it would be a lot easier to maintain all variable names in one place and just have the user switch them on/off/change the frequency rather than have the user copy and paste variable names from a database file every time they want to add a new one. The current method requires extra files and is prone to copy errors. I developed an example of a new approach within a single text file. 

- How does Hi-sAFe deal with 365 vs. 366 in the annualCells output profile? All annual profiles are actually hard-coded to export on Jan 1 if latitude is >=0 and on Jul 1 if latitude is < 0. This is confusing and should be allowed to be more flexible.

title: Soil surface mulch decomposition
body:
There was a mysterious problem in A4 forestry. In this plot, the CELLS::carbonResidue pool flat lines after ~10 years. This coincides with when tillage stops in this system. At this point, CELLS::runOff and CELLS::soilEvaporation also go to 0. This seems to indicate that the tree leaf litter is just piling up on the soil surface, never getting incorporated because of no tillage, and never breaking down due to the bug above. Eventually the litter layer gets so thick that it effectively stops soil evaporation and runoff.  

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/48125777-c47c3b00-e27f-11e8-8c41-2ddb7e02fb50.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/48125781-c9d98580-e27f-11e8-8c55-26973511e2a8.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/48125794-d231c080-e27f-11e8-963b-84b3c1980e93.png)

After many days of investigation, we realized that the issue was quite simple: the parameters for residue decomposition on the soil surface in the stics.par file were causing surface residue decomposition to go extremely slow (e.g. it would take 5 years of bare soil for 5 t/ha of weed biomass to decompose). 

Soil evaporation goes to 0 at this point because the mulch layer is so thick. However, the mulch does intercept rain and this intercepted rain can be evaporated too. So It’s more like a tradeoff of where the evaporated water is coming from. We will now export CELLS::mulchEvaporation and add that into the water cycle calculations. 

Soil CELLS::runOff also goes to 0 at this point because qmulchruis0 parameter (amount of mulch above which runoff is suppressed) for the tree leaf residue compartment is also set to 1 t/ha. 

For a temporary “fix”, we applied the decomposition parameter for INSIDE the soil to the soil surface compartments. This effectively sped up the decomposition and got rid of the mulch build-up issue. HOWEVER, we are unsure if these parameters are sound when applied to the soil surface. We will try to find a stics.par file from someone who has run multi-year STICS simulations and would hopefully have reasonable values.

It turns out that other STICS people have had this issue as well – they just reset the mulch biomass every year and don't carry over from year to year! 

Some references from the literature for perspective: 
McClaugherty et al. (1988) show 5-5.5 t/ha of mulch biomass in temperate hardwood forests in WI. 
Vogt et al. (1986) show 8-9  4 (SE) t/ha for temperate and subtropical deciduous forest.

LATEST situation is better (see below). However, it would be ideal to actually have parameters that were selected specifically for aboveground decomposition, rather than just stealing the belowground ones and calling it good.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/48125866-00170500-e280-11e8-8d9c-ce277befab24.png)

title: What value for the Transpiration Coefficient of the trees ?
body:
The TC coefficient has a strong impact on tree water needs, and subsequently on tree growth. 

In the parameter calibration, we included TC in the parameterization, and the best solution had TC=3.3. This value was by far higher than the standard value that we used previously (1.2)

The DBH of trees at age 50 (plot A2) is 52 cm with TC = 1.2 and 40 cm with TC = 3.3.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/77773189-8b499400-7049-11ea-8212-db228d06e197.png)

The explanation is simple : with TC=3.3, the water needs are much higher (+80 to 100%), the soil water resource is exhausted sooner, high levels of water stress are predicted, resulting in low C acquisition, and a strong reduction of the tree leaf area the next year. this impact occurs only when the soil is fully explored by the root system, after year 2020

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/77774286-1a0ae080-704b-11ea-9051-68bed33fd043.png)

In the 50 year simulation of plot A2 in Restinclières that we use for assessing the impact of large trees on crop yield, we used this TC = 3.3. This induces high levels of water stress in the trees when the trees colonize the full soil thickness (6 m). A high level of water stress in year Y makes tree leaf plummet during year Y+1, reducing the light competition with the crop. 

Are these high levels of water stress for the walnut trees sensible? Time will tell... I already observed mature walnut trees with very low leaf areas in dry years at other places (like the "Pont du renard" walnut plantation at Notre-Dame de Londres) where the soil is shallow and no water table available.

My gut feelings is that with TC=3.3, the behaviour of the trees is too hectic. Stress indexes are by far too high. But what if we underestimate the tree rooting depth? We probably should run a simulation with an infinte soil depth to see what is the maximum depth that the tree root system can reach. However, tte water table will kill a lot of fine roots each winter at depths.

However, this reduction of tree growth with TC=3.3 does not explain the low impact of the trees on the crop yield. With TC=1.2 (and bigger trees), the impact of the trees on the crop yield is again very low 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/77774596-a61d0800-704b-11ea-8e4e-f9d0425e3416.png)

title: Calculating crop stress indexes during specific crop phenological stages
body:
The avoidance of some crop stresses tyanks to the trees may be a key facilitative mechanism in alley-cropping.

We are questioning if the trees could protect the crops against some abiotic stresses such as frost, heat, water shortage. and, why not, nitrogen shortage (as a result of the tree litter recycling?)

To address this question, we need to calculate the stress indexes during specific phenological stages of the crop.

We can identify the following stresses/stages combinations :

frost during LEV-AMF (impact on plant density)
frost during LAT-FLO (impact on grain number)
frost during FLO-REC (impact on grain number)

heat during LAT-FLO (impact on grain number)
heat during FLO-MAT (impact on grain filling)

Water stress during LEV-AMF (impact on leaf area and biomass)
Water stress during AMF-LAX (impact on leaf area and biomass)
Water stress during LAT-FLO (impact on grain number)

More [stress;stages] combination may be relevant : we need to read again carefully the STICS red book.

To compare simulations (and especially MC and AF), we need integrated values of stress during the crop stages. These stages may not be synchronized as the phenology is different in MC and in AF (and in each cell of the scene in AF, resulting in average values of phenology at the plot scale that are not integers.)

Daily crop indexes are values in the [0;1] range. Some stress indexes like FTEMPREMP (temperature stress during grain filling) are boolean (0 or 1).

For stress indexes with numerical values between 0 (full stress) and 1 (no stress), a measure of the stress can be obtained by an average of the daily values, if the impact of the stress is multiplicative on the mechanisms

For stress indexes with boolean values (0 or 1), the average value may not be a good metrics. Usually the stress impact is multiplicative on a process (eg : FTEMPREMP). Therefore, the impact is higher during a day when the process is high : a better metrics would be a weighted average using the value of the process as a weighting factor.

How can we get these integrated stress values in the outputs? Two options : 

- calculated by HisAFe and included in the output files
- calculated by routines (R or Excel) with the output files

What is needed to do the calculations :

- the daily values of the stress indexes
- the dates of the changes of phenological stages

In the plot outputs, the phenological stages are blurred as the different cells have different phenological rythms. The calculations should be done in the cell output.

The usual plot output includes so far 8 daily stress indexes (I consider only the mainCrop)

MainCropNitrogenBiomassStress
MainCropNitrogenLaiStress
MainCropNitrogenSenescenceStress
MainCropNitrogenStress
MainCropWaterStress
MainCropTurgescenceWaterStress
MainCropSenescenceWaterStress

No frost or temperature stress is included.

The usual cell output included only 2 daily stress indexes

HisafeWaterStress
HisafeNitrogenStress

but we added recently 12 indexes :

SticsWaterSenescenceStress
SticsWaterStomatalStress
SticsWaterTurgescenceStress
SticsNitrogenBiomassStress
SticsNitrogenLaiStress
SticsNitrogenSenescenceStress
NitrogenNutritionIndex
TempStressLUE
TempStressGrainFilling
FrostStressPlantDensity
FrostStressFoliage
FrostStressReprod

The integrated stress indexes will provide only one value for each phenological stage. It will not be convenient to add these values in the current plot or cell outputs. Can we consider a .stress output file that could be structured as follows :

            StressIndex1 StessIndex2 StressIndex3........
stage1
stage2
stage3
.
.
.

Or alternatively, a R script could transform the .cell ouput in such a file?
Francesco, how did you manage this issue?
Thanks for your suggestions.

title: What value for the tcxstop parameter for durum wheat?
body:
I spotted a strange value for the tcxstop parameter for durum wheat.

TCXSTOP is the threshold of crop temperature that stops the calculation of the sum of degree-days for predicting the phasic development of the crop (phenology). Cf RedBook p31. The sum of degree days is calculated between TCMIN and TCMAX as TCROP-TCMIN. When TCROP >TCMAX, the sum is increased by a decreasing linear function between TCMAX and TCXSTOP. The redbook clearly states that this TCXSTOP parameter is important to model the impact of climate change on crops, and obviously also to model the impact of tree shade on crops!

In the current durum wheat parameters, we have TCXSTOP=100° celsius (and TDMIN=0°; TDMAX=28°). This is strange and not much sensible. In the redbook (p31), TCXSTOP= 35° for wheat. Durum wheat is a mediterranean species that is probably more adapted to heat than soft wheat. But assuming that TCXSTOP=100° means that at TCROP=30°, the impact of heat is negligible. 

A fast check of the 50 year run at the A2 MC plot shows that
in April, the crop temeprature never exceeds 21°
in May, the crop temperature never exceeds 28° 
in June (graph below), the crop temperature exceeds 28° almost every year, and 30° 16 years among 24 (2/3) in the sun.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/79242298-6db36180-7e74-11ea-817a-bc7f54388c63.png)

Using a threshold to slow the growth with high temperature will therefore have an impact only during the phenological stages that occur in June : the grain filling. Using TCXSTOP=35 instead of tcxstop=100 will slow the process and make the grain filling stage longer in the shade.

I suggest to use the TCXSTOP=35°c for durum wheat, and to check the impact on wheat behaviour by comparing two runs with TCXSTOP = [35;100] both in MC and AF (with large final trees : 50 year run using LUEmax=0.65 or 22 year run with boosted tree growth using LUEmax=1.3)

title: Why is the second option for calculating crop transpiration not available in HisAFe?
body:
Stics offers two options for calculating crop transpiration 

- The crop coefficient approach (§7.2.1)
- The resistance approach following ShuttleWorth and Wallace (§7.2.2)

The switch between the two option is controlled by the **codebeso** parameter (1 = Crop Coefficient; 2 = Resistance).

Within HisAFE, when codebeso=2, no transpiration and no soil evaporation is computed, and therefore no water stress can occur, while the crop still grows normally.

title: What values to use for crop root depth parameters?
body:
@cdupraz, in our discussion of the crop water parameter calibration, you mentioned the parameter `croirac` having a value of 0.8. I was surprised by this because we have been using a value of 1.1 for durum wheat. Before my time at INRA, the value was actually 2.0. In my "notebook" that I left you, there is a lengthy discussion about how we arrived at this new value. We should review this and make sure we are still okay with a value of 1.1 for `croirac`. **More importantly, I wonder if this "mini-optimization" that I ran to determine `croirac` based on an expected maximum rooting depth of 1.5m should be performed again after calibration of the water parameters since it seems to influence yield so much.**

Here are the notes from my 2017-2018 "notebook" regarding `croirac`. I am not sure exactly what date this was written, but it was probably spring 2018:

---------------------EXCERPT FROM NOTEBOOK----------------------------------------------

The `obstarac` parameter (which sets a maximum rooting depth of the crop) has been set to 1.2 in all HISAFE .pld files that I have personally ever seen. While chatting one day, we decided to effectively release this restriction by setting `obstarac` to 10. I did this and didn't really think about it anymore. It turns out, this has caused a huge problem. When the crop roots are not forced to stay in shallow soil, our wheat explores much deeper soil, grows much larger, and extracts all of the mineral nitrogen from the soil! What first caused me to notice this is that all of a sudden the tree roots were never colonizing any voxels under the mainCrop - they stayed within the interCrop. This is because there was no nitrogen under the mainCrop!

In the plot below, you can see a virtual experiment where I varied `obstarac` from 1 to 6 (the bottom of the soil profile). You can see that the impact changes each year, but overall the impact on yield is huge. 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/85318629-ebec3f80-b485-11ea-99d9-326cbe1454ac.png)

I asked Eric Justes about this, and he said that I should look at the .plt parameter that controls the downward growth of roots in STICS: `croirac`. He said that that if we want roots to not grow as much, then we need to reduce this parameter. He also said that our current value of 0.2 in the durum-wheat file is "crazy". This value of 0.2 is also mentioned explicitly in the Talbot thesis. So, I ran a second virtual experiment to test the impact of `croirac` when `obstarac` is set to 10. Maximum rooting depth is DEFINITELY affected, but it would take an unrealistically small value of `croirac` to get the ideal rooting depth (measured in the field) of ~1.5m. Furthermore, ALL of the 10+ wheat cultivar .plt files we have on hand had `croirac` as 0.19 or 0.2. 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/85318766-2b1a9080-b486-11ea-9f0a-6565dbd8ea64.png)

Christian asked Marie from the STICS team about this, and she suggested checking the `stoprac` parameter, which sets the phenological phase in which root growth stops. We had this set to “sen”, which means that roots grow all the way until plant death. Marie, as well as a quick literature search, suggested that this should actually be set to “lax” for durum wheat, so that root growth stops once flowering starts. After doing this and re-running the second virtual experiment from above, it becomes clear that a `croirac` value of ~0.11 (which is around what Eric Justes originally said was reasonable) gives an average max rooting depth of ~1.5 m. 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/11711566/85318829-42f21480-b486-11ea-83d3-6c7f0d37883f.png)

**Moving forward, we will use `croirac` = 0.11, `cropRootObstruction` (`obstarac`) = 10 (off), and `stoprac` = lax.**

---------------------EXCERPT FROM NOTEBOOK----------------------------------------------

title: Macroporosity & crop sensitivity to anoxia
body:
Continuing to post a few issues here based on some notes that I found from the end of my time at INRA....

In our current simulations, is anoxia is having an impact on wheat growth? We want it to! In fall 2011, wheat is planted on DOY 291 (Oct 18), after which is there > 250mm of rain in just a week or two. This situation likely created some intense water logging which _may_ have then been the cause of the ultimately low yield in spring 2012. The model is NOT predicting this low yield in spring 2012, so perhaps the model is not adequately accounting for the impact of anoxia on the early wheat growth that season. 

According to the RedBook, sensanox, which is the main parameter controlling crop sensitivity to anoxia, should be 1 for wheat (maximum sensitivity). This is what we are using. SO, if there is an issue here, it could be that the model is not “determining” that the conditions are waterlogged/anoxic, so the stress sensitivity cannot even play out (this is illustrated by anox(z), which is 0 if not saturated and 1 if saturated). What would have to change to trigger the “determination” of waterlogged conditions? We likely need to export exofac and anox (by layer) from STICS so that we can explore this.

Finally, if I read the RedBook correctly, all of the above is actually only possible if **macroporosity** is turned on - without this, saturated conditions are not possible. **We currently have macroporosity off in all simulations.** Ifthere is still not enough/a lot of saturation after turning macroporosity on, then we can try to decrease the infiltrability.

title: The case of Finert : can we convert a parameter into a variable?
body:
Finert is the fraction of the humus that is inert, which means that it is not degraded by mineralisation.

In a standard short term simulation, Finert is a parameter. It depends on the kind of humus in the soil. Forest soils have a lower finert parameter than cropped soil (redbook page 145). Heavy organic fertilisation (organic manure) induce lower Finert values (redbook page 145).

In a long term simulation (10 to 100 years) , we could consider that Finert could change, especially in agroforestry. Finert could become a variable, changing at the year time step. Are they any variables in Stics that change at the year time step?

What could drive the change in Finert? The quality of the litters and amendments that bring organic matter that is transformed into the soil humus. This quality could be described by the C/N ratio of the litters and amendments. This is probably not enough : tree litters are rich in lignin and polyciclic compounds that induce different humification and mineralisation patterns.

The default value of Finert is 65% in Stics. It could get lower if we move to a more "foret" humus in agroforestry. Could we imagine an equation predicting the change in finert as a consequence of the quality of the litters and manure during the previous year?

title: Documenting the changes in species parameters : a new policy in HisAFe
body:
The problem : during an investigation on some unsensible predictions of the model (for walnut growth at Restinclières), we discovered that more than 20 different parameter sets for walnut trees were used since 2008. 

We created a database of these sets of parameters, allowing to trace exactly when some parameters were changed.

However, the reasons for the changes were not documented. In most cases, we did not find any explanations for the change of these parameters.

The issue became serious when we realized that most of the problems that we were facing (such as unexplained growth stop of the trees or irrealistic stem/coarse root ratios) were in fact due to some changes in parameters.

The only solution to prevent such erratic moficications with unexpected and undocumented effects, (and the huge loss of time associated) demands 3 actions to be completed each time a parameter is changed

1. documenting systematically any change in any parameter : who? why? when? With what control of the impact?.
2. renaming the parameter file after each change using a Version number (eg : walnut_V23.tree)
3. controlling that the new set of parameters does not introduce unwanted consequences by running a standard simulation and checking outputs.

You will find the history of the walnut parameters in the following Excel file
[Database of walnut parameters.xlsx](https://github.com/hisafe/hisafe/files/5695613/Database.of.walnut.parameters.xlsx)

You will find a synthesis of the evolution of each parameter in the following file
[Evolution of walnut parameters.xlsx](https://github.com/hisafe/hisafe/files/5695623/Evolution.of.walnut.parameters.xlsx)

Please update any future change in the walnut set of parameters in the following file 
[Walnut parameters since 2021.xlsx](https://github.com/hisafe/hisafe/files/5695637/Walnut.parameters.since.2021.xlsx)

After a detailed study of the impact of many walnut parameters, it was decided to step back to the Talbot parameters dated 19/12/2011, with some updated parameters when the motives for updating were known. A new calibration of the current version of the model is scheduled in early 2021 and will help to define better some key parameters.

title: Can HisAFe predict the death of the crop from water stress? The swfacmin = 0 issue
body:
With the new version of HisAFe, the crop stomatal water stress is calculated by the water sharing routine of HisAFe, not by STICS. It results in the hisafewaterstress variable that replaces the SWFAC variable of STICS. This stress variable controls the dayly biomass increment (multiplication)

The SWfacmin parameter (in the stics.par file) is a minimum threshold for this stress variable. We had fixed that parameter to 0.1. This meant that each time the water uptake was less than 10% of the water demand, the swfac variable was maintained at 0.1, and the biomass increment was also maintained to 10% of the potential one. 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/105338069-68412f80-5bdb-11eb-976c-90911687e12e.png)

This resulted in unsensible water use efficiency values!

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/105338146-827b0d80-5bdb-11eb-80a1-07311daaeaee.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/105338245-9e7eaf00-5bdb-11eb-9889-62a772b12b8c.png)

The reason for not allowing swfac to go below 0.1 is not clear. It was an unwise feeling that too intense stresses are not manageable by the crop. But they are, at least in the model.

If the rooting depth of the crop is shallower than the evaporationMaxDepth parameter (= 60 cm in our sets), and if the soil moisture falls under the wilting point in all these layers, the water uptake will fall to 0, as the stress index. This is the death for most plants that do need to transpire a minimum to stay alive (and not reach deadly temperatures). So far, the model do not predict death, and the growth will resume as soon as some water is brought back into the soil and uplift the soil moisture above the wilting point.

When a crop is rooted below the evaporationMaxDepth = 60 level, the soil moisture can never fall below the wilting point, but only tends asymptotally to reach the wilting point with time. The plant can never die from water stress in that case. This is what will happen with all trees and most crops.

We could of course code the death of a plant in HisAFe. It could happen when the water stress falls below a threshold, maybe for a number of consecutive days? In that case, the growth should not happen again when the water stress is relieved. How can we make it? Putting the biomass to 0? Changing the phenology ?

title: Synchronising the automatic irrigation of the crop on all the cells of a HisAFe scene
body:
**How to manage automatic irrigation of a HisAFe scene?**

All cells of a HisAFe scene are independent, and the automatic irrigation calculation will provide different times and doses of irrigation on each cell. This is of course not possible for the farmer, irrigation is done at the same time on the whole alley.
How could we trigger irrigation at the same time on all the cells?

First option : Built-in HisAFe automatic irrigation
We decide for a “leading” cell. Automatic irrigation will be calculated on that cell (codecalirrig = 1) and applied to all the cells of the scene. Is that possible with the HisAFe structure? We need a code analysis. Should the user decide what is the leading cell? Or can we leave it to be decided automatically, for example based on the light distribution on the cells?

Second option : Two simulation steps adjusted irrigation.
We first run HisAFe with the automatic irrigation option. We choose again a leading cell, and save the irrigation scheme in the irrigation parameters ( .tec file). This would require a different .tec file for each year. We then use the codecalirrig = 2 option with a new run.

In a methodological approach, I have compared a simulation with independent irrigation on each cell (maize) for the automatic option, and common fixed irrigation with the prescribed irrigation option. The small differences between the two options at the plot scale (yield, biomass, etc…) are encouraging.
 

**More details about automatic irrigation in Stics.** 

3 parameters control automatic irrigation :

P_codecalirrig | automatic calculation of irrigation   requirements: yes (2), no (1)
P_codlocirrig | code of irrigation localisation: 1= above   the foliage, 2= below the foliage above the soil, 3 = in the soil
P_codedate_irrigauto | option to activate the beginning and the ending date in case of automatic irrigation  : yes (1), no (2)

The default parameter set of maize includes :
effirr = 1.00000 (irrigation efficiency : 1 means that all water is used)
codecalirrig = 2 (irrigation at prescribed dates and doses)
ratiol = 0.00000 (value of the SWFAC water stress ratio that triggers irrigation)
dosimx = 40.00000 (maximum irrigation dose)
doseirrigmin = 20.00000 (minimum irrigation dose)
codedateappH2O = 2 (no starting and ending dates for irrigation)
#nap = 10 (fixed calendar with 10 irrigations)
#178	20.00 ; #185	25.00 ; #192	30.00 ; #199	30.00 ; #206	30.00 ; #213	20.00 ; #220	20.00 ; #227	20.00 ; #234	20.00 ; #241	20.00 
codlocirrig = 1 
locirrig = 0 (depth of underground irrigation)

codedateappH2O is equivalent to codedate_irrigauto. If we activate codedate_irrigauto (codedate_irrigauto = 1), the beginning and ending dates of irrigation are datedeb_irrigauto and datefin_irrigauto (parameters located in stics.par in ## TEMPOPARV6 section)

Activating the automatic calculation of irrigation needs codecalirrig = 1 
I have assumed ratiol=0.5 (SWFAC gets often below that threshold in our situation with/without irrigation)?

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/105675712-c6c32200-5ee9-11eb-9fd3-494e8f56d2ae.png)

**A concerning problem appears :** often two irrigations happen during two consecutive days. The first irrigation is not enough to raise swfac above the threshold tye next day (0.5 in this example). For this reason a second irrigation is calculated the next day, resulting in two irrigations during two consecutive days. This is not very satisfactory, as it results in 80 mm of irrigation in two days. To reduce this amount, I tried to fix the maximum amount of one irrigation at 30 mm. It did not reduce the occurrence of double irrigation (as expected), but it did also not reduce the total amount of irrigation, and this was more surprising. I finally kept the 40 mm maximum for one irrigation.

Could it be possible to prevent two irrigations to occur during two consecutive days? A simple test could be added in the Stics code with an index of irrigation the previous day. It would hopefully give the required time to SWFAC to rise above the threshold (to be confirmed).


The final parameters for automatic calculation of irrigation of maize are then :
codecalirrig = 1
ratiol=0.5
codedate_irrigauto = 2 (no limit dates for te start and end of irrigation)
dosimx = 40
doseirrigmin = 20
irrlev=20 triggers a 20 mm irrigation at germination. 

NOTE : irrlev is in Stics.par! It applies to all crops when codecalirrig=1. It would be more logical to have irrlev in the .tec file, and that irrlev is applied irrespective of the codecalirrig option, to secure the germination. If irrlev is applied only when codecalirrig=1, it means that when codecalirrig = 2 (prescribed irrigation) you need to include a prescribed irrigation at germination in case of dry conditions. But you don't know when the germination will occur... So irrlev should be applied at the planting date?

Is it possible that the irrigation at germination happens only if it is useful? Is it cancelled if we choose codedate_irrigauto = 1 and 
datedeb_irrigauto > date of potential germination

**Summary of the work to be done** 

1. Synchronizing automatic irrigation on all the cells of the scene
2. Preventing irrigation on two consecutive days
3. Controlling irrigation at germination when colcalirrig=1

title: Residues incorporation for perenial crops is wrong
body:
The simulation of annual crops with Stics implies that the soil is bare before seeding or after harvesting (depending on the harvest settings).

This is not sensible in many cases. We often have weeds or natural vegetation growing between crops, This vegetation has an impact on many processes : capture of nitrates that would otherwise lixiviate, additional biomass that will be incorporated in the soil  by tilling for the next crop or that will provide a mulch on the soil.

We therefore decided to create a "weed" crop that is based on the wheat model. This "weed" crop is well adapted to simulate the dynamics of weeds that have a phenology close to wheat : germination in autumn, slow growth during winter, fast growth in early spring, end of cycle before summer. 

But when we use this "weed" crop, we often stop the simulation well before the "harvest" time. The weed crop is stopped by the start of the next crop. In that case, no harvest occurs, and the biomass accumulated by this "weed" crop is lost. This is not acceptable. This biomass should be incorporated as a residue. This has a deleterious impact on the nitrogen stock in the soil : all the nitrogen captured by the weeds is lost.

A similar issue occurs in forestry simulations or on the tree strip of agroforestry plots. If we use an annual weed crop to simulate the natural vegetation, the biomass and nitrogen captured is lost. When cumulated over decades, this has a disastrous impact on the whole system, with N deficiency and stress for both crops and trees. In that case, we decided to use a perennial grass instead of an annual weed crop. Perennial grass is managed with cuttings. But the biomass cut is also supposed to be exported by Stics. This has the same deleterious impact on the C and N budget of the soil. Cuttings should be incorporated as residues, not incorporated.

We need to solve this issue

title: Add topping of trees (reduction of tree height, including pollarding)
body:
Several tree management schemes include topping of trees. Topping means reducing the tree height by cutting the trunk and/or all branches above a given height. After topping, the tree looks like a table (flat top). If topping is done below the canopy, this is called pollarding. Topping is usual with many fruit tree species such as olive trees.

After topping, the tree stem is no longer a cone, but a truncated cone. Let's call the diameter at topping height DTH.

The tree DBH is not affected by topping, but the tree height is reduced. The tree is imbalanced, and the growth algorithm will induce fast growth in height. This is sensible and is observed on topped trees.

However, several equations on the Safe tree model are not fit to manage a truncated cone. This is true with the stem volume allometry that predicts the stem volume from tree height and DBH (to allow for non conical tree trunks). This equation should be modified.

What will be the shape of the trunk after regrowth after topping? It should be a cone piled on a truncated cone. This is not easy to manage.. We could assume that it remains a truncated cone with the same conicity as the basl part of the trunk. In that case, the diameter at the top of the tree will not be zero until the regrowth reached the previous height, or a higher position, as the tree DBH will keep growing.

This would mean that a new variable should be added to describe the tree : the DTT (Diameter at the tree top). For an untopped tree, DTT = 0 and the tree trunk is assumed to be a cone. For a topped tree, DTT=DTH on the day of topping. Then it will change with tree height and DBH.

With this change, the SAFE tree algorithm should be able to manage both tree topping and tree pollarding. It should also be able to manage shrubs : annual topping will keep the shrub size in the desired range.

title: Tree topping
body:
Tree topping consists in reducing the height of a tree. It is usually achieved by cutting both the main stem and the branches above the topping level. 

Here is an example with olive trees :

![IMG_0001](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/136531211-c23a7b54-10eb-4c49-845a-3301b9d81554.JPG)

When topping involves removing all tree branches, we call it pollarding. In that case, the trunk may be cut down above the level of the base of the canopy, but all branches below are removed. Pollarding may therefore be described as both topping and pruning up to the topping height.

Topping is quite usual for fruit trees (apple trees, cherry trees) or fodder trees (Mulberry, Ash, Willows, etc..). It is also a standard management for shrubs or Short Rotation Coppice (SRC), where the trees are cut down to the soil level. 

Topping is a very disturbing management for the trees. The DBH / height relationship is totally violated. The stem volume / DCH / height relationship is also violated.

To allow topping in HisAFe, we need to modify the tree growth module. 

Two main challenges are to be met 

> The topped trees are far from the standard control allometries. What will the current algorithm do?
> When topping is performed below 1.3 m height, trees have no DBH. How to manage?

Right after topping, the tree stem is no longer a cone. It is a truncated cone. A tree that was never topped can be considered as a truncated cone with the upper diameter of the cone = 0. After the first growing season after topping, the tree stem is a truncated cone surmounted by a cone. After several years, it will go back to a single cone, unless a new topping occurs, as for pollards.

Can we extend the formalism of HisAFe to a truncated cone to represent the tree stem?

To manage topping below 1.3 m, could we replace DBH as a driving variable by DSL (Diameter at soil level)? DBH would still be used when Tree height > 1.3m.

@LECOMTE-ISADEV 
Can we try to top a tree and check the behaviour of the current algorithm without changing anything in the code? I suggest to run a standard Restinclières simulation and produce a .prj file at age 20. And to top the tree at age 21.

It is probably simple to add a code line that reduces tree height and tree stem volume...

title: Leaf frost stress dammage
LUE affected by leaves age and temperature
body:
We need to combine two approaches to model the LUE of evergreen trees (and deciduous trees).
1) make it thermodependent as indicated by Nicolas with the same formalism as for culture in Stics.
2) keeping it sensitive to leaf age (leaf aging), as currently coded for deciduous trees.
It is this age dependence that will make Cohort 2 and 3 leaves less effective.
For deciduous trees, leaf aging parameters lead to a zero LUEmax (for hybrid walnut) after 173 days. For a budburst on May 1 (day 121), this leads to a zero LUE on day 294 (October 21).
For evergreen trees, these parameters must be reviewed so that the LUEmax becomes zero after several years. For the olive tree, since only 3 annual cohorts are kept, the LUEmax should be canceled out after 4 years, i.e. approximately 1460 days.
To combine the 2 effects, you can calculate daily an age-dependent LUE for each cohort, then correct it by temperature.
For the carbon gain, it must therefore be done for each cohort, and then the sum to obtain the daily carbon gain of the tree.

title: Pipe drainage and watertables : how to manage pipe or ditch drainage?
body:
Watertables in the soil may be of two kinds 

1. Regional watertable : the depth of this watertable is independent of the local water balance (rain, water uptake by plants). It is imposed from outside the plot (by a river usually). The local water balance cannot modify this water table depth. When water enters the watertable by drainage, the watertable level doesn't change. Water is supposed to be lost horizontally by the watertable into the river. Regional watertables depths are included in the weather file and thier levels are imposed to the whole simulated scene.

2. Local watertable : the depth of this local watertable is linked to the local water balance. Water accumulates on top of an impermeable (or low permeable) layer and saturates macroporosity. The watertable rise will occur after heavy rains, and water table recessions are caused by root uptake (and soil evaporation if the watertable is close to the top). Local watertable depth is calculated by STICS when macroporosity = 1

Artificial drainage is well managed by Stics with local watertables (macroporosity = 1 and artificialDrainage =1). It is necessary to define the depth of an impermeable layer above which water will accumulate and saturate soil horizons. 

But the problem is how to simulate artificial drainage with a regional watertable?

We can consider two options when activating artificial drainage with a permanent watertable 

1. No watertable and an impermeable layer at the depth where the watertable is always present. 

2. Activate the watertable but clip the watertable depth at the level of the drains (pipes or ditches). 

In the second option, a fast rise in the regional watertable above the pipes or ditches level will be cancelled, as if the drains were able to drain all the rising water. This is of course an approximation.

In a monocrop scene, the Hooghoudt equation included in STICS predicts the quantity of water drained each day by the pipes, and the level of the watertable is then adjusted. Simple and easy. The model assumes a unique watertable depth, while in reality it will depend from the distance to the pipe. 

In an agroforestry scene, on each cell, the same equation will be used, resulting in different watertable depths in each cell (as water uptake by plants is different on each cell, hence water content of the soil is also different). But the distance to the pipes or ditches will not be taken into account.

If, for example, the pipes are in the middle of the cropped alley, the level of the watertable should be higher on the tree lines than in the middle of the alley. This is not possible to predict with HisAFe. Stics will calculate the depth of the watertable in each cell, small differences may occur due to differences in water uptake by roots of crops and trees. The watertable will therefore be at different depths in the different cells. This is why the first option with no watertable but an impermeable layer is probably more adapted to HisAFe. It may predict that the watertable could be deaper below the trees than in the alley. In nature, this would be levelled by horizontal flows of water, but this is not available in HisAFe : we could design an algorithm that would level off the local watertable depth on the scene by calculating the average depth of the watertable, assuming some horizontal flows of water between cells.

title: Virtual cancellation of competition for light, water or nitrogen by the trees
body:
What is the limiting process in the tree-crop system? Light? Water? Nitrogen? And when? This is a crux question.

HisAFe could help to provide deep insights into this question.

An elegant option would be to do virtual simulations with trees that do not capture light or uptake water or uptake Nitrogen, but grow as if they were. In that case, the crops would face compétition only for the "competition on" ressources. 

Such a simulation would of course not be consistent : trees growing without water uptake (or nitrogen uptake, or light capture) are of course chimeric. These simulations would be useful only as a baseline to compare with full simulations including all the competition processes.

Cancelling light competition : Crop irradiation under the trees is set back to the standard value.
Cancelling water competition : Tree water uptake is set to zero in the soil update
Cancelling Nirogren competition : Tree Nitrogen Uptake is set to zero in the soil update.

Everything else should remained unchanged, including the tree growth, as the target is to compare the growth of crops under exactly the same trees.

But there is a difficulty there : If the water uoptake is cancelled, the next day, the water content of the soil will be different, and therefore, the tree growth will be different. To obtain exactly the same tree we need to run the simulation twice : a first run will provide all the tree variables (above and belowground) when all the competitions are "on".

A "competion off" simulation can then be run. To obtain the same trees during this simulation, , we need to force all tree variables daily. 
This is probably not as simple as it seems.

title: High density tree stands : Tree Self Pruning and enhanced height growth
body:
So far, the height growth of trees in HisAFe is not stimulated when tree to tree competition for light is high. This should be corrected, as it happens always in forestry stands with high densities of trees. It could also happen in Agroforestry stands when the trees get big and when their canopies become coaslescent.

Light competition between trees has two major impacts : faster height growth and slower diameter growth, and death of very shaded branches at the bottom of the canopy. This process is called self-pruning.

HisAFe provides all the information needed to simulate with simple formalisms both processes. 

The Light Competition Index (LCI) calculated by the light module of HisAFe will drive the two processes. LCI is the ratio between the radiation intercepted by a tree with neighbours to the radiation that it would intercept if he had no neighbours (but exactly the same Shape and leaf area). It is an excellent estimate of light competition. An isolated tree will have a LCI value of 1, all year round. A very sahded tree will have values below 0.5, meaning that 50% of the incoming radiation is intercepted by its neighbours. only the top of the canopy is in full sun. 

Here is the LCI for a forestry poplar stand with tree spacings of 5x5, 7x7 and 9x9 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/198066941-d6ab324c-194e-48b6-96b9-e6acd2ef9111.png)

Here is the detail of the variations of LCI during a year

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44842372/198067163-f06627d8-248e-4372-8acf-3f8d8edb284d.png)

Some important facts

LCI varies with the sun elevation in the sky, ie both latitude and date in the year. When the sun gets lower in the sky in automn, LCI increases (but the tree canopy is almost stable). LCI is quite stable around the summer solstice, from may to August. With an evergreen tree species, very low values of LCI can be expected in winter.

Daily variations in the LCI index reflect sunny versus cloudy days. On sunny days, the light competition is higher. But on cloudy days, the light availability is low.

Summer stable values of LCI never drop below 0.3, which is a very high competition index. Winter values could be extremely low if the sun elevation remains very low. Values below 0.1 can be expected for evergreen trees (Spruce, fir, cypress, holm oak).

### Self pruning of trees 

We can drive self pruning with LCI as follows

Two tree species parameters are needed for that 

LCI threshold value to induce self-pruning (**LCIthreshold1**) : a tree that is very sensitive to shade could self-prune for values around 0.7, a tree that is not too sensitive to self pruning would start for values around 0.5.

Duration (in days)  of the light starving period to trigger self pruning (**Shaded days for self-pruning**) : 

Light induced self-pruning occurs only after a long period of cumulated shade. We should not trigger self-pruning when the LCI meets the threshold, but compute a cumulated shading index. 

For evegreen trees, heavy levels of shade in winter will not trigger self pruning, as this is normal even for wide spaced trees, due to very low sun elevations at temperate or high latitudes.

I suggest to compute a cumulated shading index as a sum of daily shading : sum(1-LCI).

sum(1-LCI) is only calculated during the growing season (when CallocatedtoGrowth >0). For evergreen trees, it is calculated only from spring equinox to automn equinox, to avoid very low winter values that may not be sensible to trigger self-pruning.

Sum(1-LCI) is only incremented on the days when LCI<LCIthreshold1

Self-pruning is triggered when Sum(1-LCI) > N * LCIthreshold1. What value for N? 

Self pruning needs a long shade, usually for several years. A growing season is about 6-8 months in temperate countries (180 to 240 days), but up to 12 months in some tropical or mild oceanic climates. For evergreen trees the duration between the two equinoxes is 6 months.

Let assume that 3 years of heavy shade are needed to trigger self-pruning. We could then use N = 3 * 6 * 30 = 540.

Self pruning will be triggered when the cumulative shade index exceeds 540 * (1-LCIthresholds).

For the sake of simplicity, self-pruning will be performed on a fixed day in winter, For example on the 31 of January.

The height of self-pruning can be fixed to 10% of the canopy height (could be a paremeter). Self-pruning can be managed exactly as man-made pruning. The height of the base of the canopy increases, C pools of branches (and leaves for evergreen trees) are reduced, A difference : the horizontal dimensions of the canopy is not changed, trees remain in touch.

After self-pruning, the LCI index will rise, and the next self-pruning may occur after some years.

If the trees are man-made pruned, self-pruning will not occur. 

### Faster height growth when tree to tree light competition is high

LCI can also induce faster height growth by allocating more carbon to the above-ground part of the tree. If this C is diverted to AG only during height growth (= phenology stage 1) it will increase leaf area and tree height. If this happens when the trees are blocked horizontally by neighbour trees, this should favour height growth as expected.

LightStress = 1-LCI. LightStress varies between 0 (LCI=1) and 1 (LCI=0). Obviously, LCI= 0 is not possible : a tree even in the shade of its neighbours, will always intercept some light. LCI commonly varies between 1 and 0.5, but may drop to 0.2 in winter for evergreen trees.

To induce an increase in C allocation to AG, we need to increase the R* = TargetLfrRatio

Here is the current code for computing R*

if(rsStress > 0.98){
                // derive vers le haut
                double RSNoStressResponsiveness = treeSpecies.getRsNoStressResponsiveness ();
                rsStress = 1  +Math.pow(getNitrogenSaturation(),1/RSNoStressResponsiveness);
                targetLfrRatio += targetLfrRatioUpperDrift*maxTargetVariation*rsStress;                
            } else {
                targetLfrRatio -= maxTargetVariation*(1-rsStress);
            }
        }

LightStress will increase the upperdrift of LfrRatio. The following modification of the calculation of rsStress is needed  

targetLfrRatio += targetLfrRatioUpperDrift * maxTargetVariation * rsStress***(1+LightStress)**

When LCI = 1 (no shade), LightStress=0 and 1+LightStress = 1
When LCI=0.5 (heavy shade), LightStress = 0.5 and 1+LightStress=1.5 resulting in a 50% increase in the change in TargetLfrRatio

In this equation, rsStress stands for the N saturation effect. The current value of RsNoStressResponsiveness = 0.02 is not appropriate at all. With this value, no impact of Nsaturation can be expected, as Math.pow(getNitrogenSaturation(),1/RSNoStressResponsiveness is always close to 1. A RsNoStressResponsiveness value of 1 is appropriate.

In most recent simulations, TargetLfrRatio is reaching the MaxTargetLfrRatio (0.75). Therefore the light competition will not be able to increase this TargetRatio. Talbot recommended a MaxTargetLfrRatio = 0.85. It is not clear why this value was changed. Simulations with MaxTargetLfrRatio = 0.9 show that a consuistant pattern is obtained, with nice patterns of increaseand decrease of the Target with various stresses. We should therefore assign MaxTargetLfrRatio = 0.9 to allow the LightStress to impact on TargetLfrRatio.

 
_NB : in the original algorithm for the functional equilibrium we modified directly the AboveGroundAllocationFactor (AGAF) with water and Nitrogen stresses. This was modified with Grégoire Talbot to impact LfrRatio (See Talbot thesis section 1.2.2.4). We could also modify the AGAF with the lightStress, but it seems more consistant to act on the LfrRatio, as suggested above._

title: How to simulate "tall" trees? (Trees that are taller than what the control allometry allows)
body:
The tree growth algorithm never allows trees to become taller than the control allometry H=a.DBH^b
This is not satisfactory : trees that compete for light do grow in height in their search for light.

With the current algorithm
When the tree is "short", it grows in height (if phenology allows)
When the tree is balanced or "tall", it grows in both DBH and H, following the allometry

During the leaf expansion phenology stage, both H adn DBH growth are allowed, but DBH growth will occur only if the tree is tall.

After the leaf expansion phenology stage, the tree grows only in DBH, and as a consequence always ends the growing season as a short tree is the leaf expansion phase is limited in time. At the start of the next growing season, a tree that has a short leaf expansion stage (such as walnut trees) is always "short" with this algorithm.

This prevents us to predict "tall" trees (trees taller than what the allometry predicts for their DBH). This prevents us to predict the impact of light competition between trees, even when we increase the TargetLeaftoFineRoot Ratio to allocate more C to the AG part of the tree. This results in a shaded tree growing faster in both DBH and H, but still respecting the allometry.

We need to relax the height growth limitation in the case of light competition between trees.

Here is the new algorithm that I suggest.

When height growth is possible (leaf expansion stage)
If tree is short, same computation as usual : DBH is unchanged and H is increased
If tree is tall, and no light competition, same computation as usual : DBH1 = DBH0+Delta1
If tree is tall and light competition (LightCompetitionIndex<1), DBH growth is reduced and Height growth is increased as follows : the previous increase of DBH Delta1 is reduced by a factor (LCI-LCImin). LCImin is the value of LCI that would prevent any growth in diameter. It is a tree species parameter. If LCI=1, (no light competition), DBH is then computed as above. If LCI is strong, DBH increase is reduced, And then Height growth is enhanced.
Delta2=Delta1 x (LCI-LCImin)/(1-LCImin)
et DBH2=DBH0+Delta2

When height growth is no longer possible (after the end of the leaves expansion phase), Height is fixed and DBH is increased to fit the new volume of stem.


We could also relax the strict rule that DBH growth is null **during the leaf expansion phase**. By doing so, we will reduce tree height growth, especially for trees with a short leaf expansion phase such as walnuts. The rule to allow DBH growth could be as follows always allowed when tree is tall (even during the leaf expansion phase)
optional when tree is short. When tree is short, a very small amount of DBH growth could be allowed, by reducing height growth by a fixed proportion (eg : 10%). This % will allow a small DBH growth to fit the StemVolume allometry.

This could be optional

title: Introducing the polycyclism of tree growth
body:
Most trees can have several flushes of growth (leaf area and height) during the same year. This is called polycyclism. The spring flush of growth is usually the most important, and in many cases, the only one. But if the conditions are favourable, some new flushes of growth may occur later.

For walnut trees, new flushes are observed when the conditions are very favourable (no water stress, no heat stress), and mainly on young trees. Old and mature trees seldom have secondary flushes, probably as they experience nitrogen deficit.

For evergreen trees like the olive trees, flushes of growth may occur any time of the year, except during scorching summer days or too cold winter days.

We suggest the following formalism

The first flush of growth (vegetativePhenology = 1) is limited in time by the leafExpansionDuration parameter (90 days for walnut). When growth ceases, vegetativePhenology = 2.

When VegettaivePhenology = 2, we assess each day if the following 4 conditions are met. If yes, we go back to VegetativePhenology = 1 and a new flush of growth in leaf area and height starts. The 4 conditions are

1. At least  MinNumberOfDaysBetweenTwoGrowthFlushes since VegetativePhenology = 2
2. Waterstress>0.95 during at least MinNumberOfDaysWithoutWaterStressToInduceANewGrowthFlush
3. NitrogenStress>0.95 durng at least MinNumberOfDaysWithoutNitrogenStressToInduceANewGrowthFlush
4. Mean daily Air Temperature between two threshold values since at least MinNumberOfDaysWithFavourableTemperatureToInduceANewGrowthFlush

Condition 1 will avoid too close flushes. A new flush usually requires a dormant period for the new shoots to start to grow
Condition 2 will allow a new flush of growth only after a long period without water stress
Condition 3 will allow a new flush of growth only after a long period without nitrogen stress
Condition 4 will cancel growth flushes during scorching summer days or cold winter days.

As soon as conditions are met to go to PhenologStage = 3 (start of leaf fall), this will stop growth, whatever the Phenological stage is (1 or 2)

We need 4 new parameterrs to trigger these flushes of growth 

MinNumberOfDaysBetweenTwoGrowthFlushes = 30
MinNumberOfDaysWithoutWaterStressToInduceANewGrowthFlush = 30
MinNumberOfDaysWithoutNitrogenStressToInduceANewGrowthFlush = 30
MinNumberOfDaysWithFavourableTemperatureToInduceANewGrowthFlush = 30

The counting of days is initiated the day when VegetativePhenology = 2 (end of the previous flush of growth)

We could  have used the same parameter for the four criteria (MinNumberOfDaysWithoutStress). but having 4 different values may help, especially if we simulate tropical trees.

For the air temperature thresholds, we can use the LUEstress parameters  (values for walnut below)

lueTemperatureStressTOptMin = 15
lueTemperatureStressTOptMax = 25

The 0.95 values may be hard coded. They simply mean that we want a period without a significant stress.

For a deciduous tree, the sequence of phenology stages will read as

0 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5 if only one growth flush (no polycyclism)
0 > 1 > 2 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5 with two flushes of growth 
and rarely
0 > 1 > 2 > 1 > 2 > 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 > 5 with three flushes of growth 

For an evergreen tree, polyclism should apply only to cohort 1. 

We will need to check the DBH increment of the tree. So far, the model does not predict any DBH increment during the first flush of growth, as the tree is "short". It may be different during the secondary flushes of growth, as the tree will be close to the allometry.

title: Allowing tree canopies to overlap
body:
In systems with different tree species, overlapping of canopies is common. This is specially the case for tropical agroforestry systems such as coffee and cocoa.

The current alogorithm of tree canopy growth does not allow overlapping. When two canopies meet, horizontal growth is blocked. This was designed for monospecific stands of trees.

Releasing this limitation in growth may have perturbating consequences on the light competition module. 

Two situations are to be considered 

overlapping without contact : the canopies are at different height and do not touch
overlapping with contact : further growth will result in interpenetration of the canopies, with some volumes (intersections of ellipsoids) filled with leaves from two different trees.

title: Tropical Trees Vegetative Phenology Module
body:
The vegetative phenology module was designed for temperate trees. This module predicts the dates of budburst, end of leaf area growth, start and end of leaf fall. This module allows to model trees with short flushes of growth or with continued growth all over the growing season. Walnut is a typical tree with a short flush of growth, while poplars are typical for a continuous growing pattern.

Some temperate trees with short growing flushes are polycyclic : they display several flushes of growth during the growing season. HisAFe is not predicting polycyclism so far.

For temperate trees, air temperature is used as the driver. Budburst is triggerred when a sum of degree.days is reached (budBurstAccumulatedTemp). This sum of degree.days starts after a given date (budBurstTempAccumulationDateStart), and the sum uses a base temperature (budBurstTempThreshold). 

For tropical trees, other processes should be considered for triggering leaf expansion. These may include:

Photoperiodic effects (but the day length in tropical countries is less variable than in temperate countries)
Drought effects for trees that flushes at the beginning of the rainy season or at the geginning of the dry season (eg Faidherbia albida)
Thermal effects

Or combinations of several of these effects.

In Equatorial  conditions with no dry season, some trees have no clear pattern and may grow any time of the year. A stochastic process could then be included.

We need to make a synthesis of the phenology of vegetative growth by tropical trees to design this phenology module.



Phenology parameters and the nominal values for hybrid walnut

budBurstAccumulatedTemp = 612
budBurstDelayMaxAfterPollaring = 28

budBurstTempAccumulationDateStart = 61
budBurstTempThreshold = 0

title: How to report tree or crop water extraction calculated by HISAFE when STICS shallow mini-layer are too dry ?
body:
J'écris en français car sinon j'y arrive pas... On traduira après s'il le faut
Il vous est peut être déjà arrivé de voir apparaitre ce message au cours d'une simulation 
**cell=x  reportWaterTree=xxxx** ou **cell=x  reportWaterCrop=xxxx**
sans trop savoir à quoi cela faisait référence.
Jusqu'à présent c'était toujours des valeurs très faibles donc moi même je n'y prétais plus attention en me disant qu'un jour j'allais m'en occuper ... 
En testant l'hévéa avec Célestine, ce message est apparu très vite et très frequement avec des valeurs inquiétantes alors je me suis penchée dessus un peu sérieusement. 

Voilà ce qui se passe pour l'eau 

Hisafe calcule les extractions d'eau dans les voxels et les passe ensuite à STICS dans les mini-couches, cellule par cellule. 
On fait une division de l'extraction du voxel par le nombre de mini-couches dans le voxel pour répartir de façon homogène. 
On vérifie juste que la mini-couche a suffisement d'eau pour ne pas descendre en dessous de l'humidité résiduelle du sol (variable STICS ha qui est commune à tout le sol)  une fois qu'on aura soustrait l'extraction de l'arbre, de la culture et l'évaporation du sol. 
S'il n'y pas assez d'eau on extrait ce qu'on peux (la culture est prioritaire) et on reporte ce qui reste à la mini-couche suivante et ainsi de suite jusqu'à la dernière mini-couche de la cellule. 
Si à la fin on a pas réussi à tout extraire pour cette cellule on affiche ce message

Pour l'azote on fait plus simple, on extrait au prorata de l'azote disponible dans la mini-cocuche par rapport au total de l'azote du voxel. Il n'y a pas de report d'une mini-couche à la suivante car on a pas fixé de limite d'extraction. 

Dans le cas de l'hévéa on a des voxels humides car il pluet tous les jours mais avec une très forte évaporation donc peu d'eau disponible dans les mini-couches superficielles. Comme on prend l'eau de façon homogène on reporte l'extraction des mini-couches seches dans celles du dessous et comme au début l'arbre est peu enraciné on arrive à ne pas reussir à extraire toute l'eau demandé (alors qu'elle est bien disponible) 

Donc je pense qu'il faut extraire l'eau au prorata de l'eau disponible (comme pour l'azote) et non plus de façon homogène. 
On peux garder le systeme du report des mini-couches car on va continuer à tester qu'on ne descend pas sous l'humidité résiduelle avec l'évaporation. Par contre je trouve pas normal de passer ce report d'un voxel au suivant car cela fausse ce qui a été calculé par le module d'extraction d'eau.

title: Tree litters mineralisation
body:
Tree litters (carbon and nitrogen) are: 
1. Leaves, branches or fruits left on the soil surface after natural death or after tree management (pruning, trimming, topping...). 
2. Fine roots and coarse roots after natural death, anoxia, root pruning or tree harvest

Roots litters are separated in 2 parts : 
1. Shallow: for roots in voxels which bottom is above soil humification depth (profhum in STICS) which is about 20cm
2. Deep: for roots in voxels which bottom is below soil humification depth

For **shallow litters** we use STICS method for residus addition on surface (**ResidusApportSurfaceSol**) using as an entry 
- maximum depth of the residue incorporation (m) 
- Fresh matter (FM) added from residue (t.ha-1) 
- C/N ratio of residue
- C content of residue  (% FM)
- Water content of residue   %FM
- Type of residue   

There is 21 types of residues in STICS  

- 1 mature crop on surface (straw, roots) 
- 2 catch crop  on surface (young plants) 
- 3 farmyard manure  on surface
- 4 compost  on surface
- 5 sewage sludge  on surface
- 6 distillery vinasse  on surface
- 7 animal horn  on surface
- 8 grapevine shoots on surface
- 9 to 10 free for new residues on surface
- 11 to 20  : same as above but under surface 
- 21: crop roots

On surface means that max depth of the residue incorporation = 1cm (first mini-couche) 
Under surface means that  max depth of the residue incorporation = Min(soil management depth,humification depth)
Residus are set form surface to deep after a soil management (done by STICS in method **ResidusMelangeSol**) 

For LEAVES we add parameters for 10 = tree leaves on surface 
For BRANCHES we use 8  = grapevine shoots
For FRUITS we use 6 = distillery vinasse 
For ROOTS we use 21 crop roots  

For LEAVES, BRANCHES FRUIT  in the first voxel we have just to call ResidusApportSurfaceSol to let the residues in the first mini-couche as a mulch and after the soil management, residues will be incorporated to deeper types associated (6=>16;  8=>18; 10=>20) and mineralized. 

for ROOTS in voxel bellow humificationDepth Aurélien QUERE wrote a specific module in Hi-sAFe called **deepSenescentRootsMineralization**.  This module is inspired by STICS V5 mineralization method.  
Voxels bellow humification depth are scanned to check is there is dead roots (fine roots or coarse roots) and a mineralisation process is called and values are affected in STICS minicouches (nit and amm tables)
Here is the code for each voxel:
FMIN1 = 6e-04   //stics general parameter
FMIN2 = 0.0272  //stics general parameter
FMIN3 = 0.0167  //stics general parameter
//humidity factor 
fh = 0.80*((Theta-WiltingPoint)/(FieldCapacity-WiltingPoint))+0.20		
//température factor 
ft = Math.pow((-0.566+0.62*Math.exp(0.9125*SoilTemperature/15)),1.026)
kpot = FMIN1 /(FMIN2 +argi)/(FMIN3 +calc)
k = kpot * fh * ft
//CumulatedTreeNitrogenRootsSen = sum of tree Nitrogen FR and CR senescence for this VOXEL
nMinFromRootSen= k * CumulatedTreeNitrogenRootsSen
//Desagregation of HISAFE voxels nitrogen content in STICS miniCouches
for (int z=MiniCoucheMin; z <= MiniCoucheMax; z++) {
        nit[z+1] += (nMinFromRootSen * 10000/cellArea/miniCoucheNumber)		//from kg to kg.ha-1
        amm[z] += (nMinFromRootSen * 10000/cellArea/miniCoucheNumber);		//from kg to kg.ha-1
}
CumulatedTreeNitrogenRootsSen = CumulatedTreeNitrogenRootsSen - nMinFromRootSen

title: Adding pedotransfert parameters as optional direct inputs
body:
We wanted to apply hi-sAFe to a tropical plot, but the integrated pedotransfert functions were developed for Europe only (Wösten et al., 1998, DOI: 10.1016/S0016-7061(98)00132-3). 
We considered several options:
- integrate other pedotransfert functions for other regions and let the user chose between them,
- include, as inputs, the parameters of van Genuchten-Mualem formulas (i.e. theta sat, Ksat, alpha, lambda, n) and bulk density.

Since the studied plot had calibrated van Genuchten-Mualem parameters and measured bulk density, we chose the latter. It is thus now possible to add directly the pedotransfert parameters and the bulk density. If known, hi-sAFe will use them, otherwise they will be calculated using the Wösten formulas.

title: [Faidherbia phenology] Leaf fall lasts one day and new budburst is triggered immediately
body:
Hi!
Phenology for Faidherbia was implemented (see https://github.com/hisafe/hisafe/issues/177#issuecomment-3790899099) but delivers unusual results:
- `leafFallStartingDate` sometimes is triggered one day after `leafExpansionEndingDate`, when there should be a period of 95 days between the two (`budBurstToLeafFallDuration` minus `leafExpansionDuration`),
- then, `leafFallEndingDate` can happen one day afterwards too,
- a new budburst can be triggered the day after.
This happens when leaf fall starts at the end of the year, for instance in December.

## Example of outputs:

```
28/12*************LeafFallStartingDate=362
JulianDay=363 Date=29/12/2021
+++++++++++++++++ Reduction of leafFallTest
29/12*************LeafFallEndingDate=363
leafFallTest: 147
JulianDay=364 Date=30/12/2021
JulianDay=365 Date=31/12/2021
31/12*************BudburstDate=365 lastBudburst=251 waterTableDay=266
```

## Why it happens
"+++++++++++++++++ Reduction of leafFallTest" indicates that the following was triggered and applied:
```
if (leafFallTest > nbrDays) {
	leafFallTest = leafFallTest - nbrDays;
	System.out.println("+++++++++++++++++ Reduction of leafFallTest");
}
```

Because leafFallTest is corrected this way, if leaf fall starts at the end of the year (for instance DOY = 364, so 29/12), the recalculated leafFallTest is always smaller than the current day, since it's supposed to be early in the next year. As after recalculation, we indeed have `julianDay >= leafFallTest`, the code then goes straight to the next phenological stage, i.e. leaf fall finished. 

Then, it testes weather a new budburst should be triggered, and since the same recalculation happens for lastBudburst (see below), the test is cleared if it happens late during the year.
```
if (lastBudburst > nbrDays) lastBudburst = lastBudburst - nbrDays;
```

## Fixes
I see two solutions, both aiming at changing the leafFallTest recalculation:
1. Either create counters (i.e. when entering a new phenological stage, trigger a counter that +1 for every day until it reaches `budburstDelayFromLastBudburst` or `leafFallDuration`), so it does not rely on DOY, 
2. Either include a test on the year (i.e. something like `if (leafFallTest > nbrDays), then leafFallTest = leafFallTest - nbrDays and yearToCompare = currentYear +1; else yearToCompare = currentYear` then `if (julianDay >= leafFallTest and yearToCompare = currentYear)`), so that it relies on both DOY and year.

I do not know which one would be more suitable to existing code. What do you think @LECOMTE-ISADEV? Tell me if you want my input files to test this out, I can drop them in U:\.

Wrong unit displayed in comments for bulk density
body:
In SafePedotransferUtil, bulkDensity is said to be calculated in kg/m3 (l. 247). I think it actually is in g/cm3 according to
1. the source material ([Stolte, Wessling et Wösten, 1996](https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/pedotransfer-functions-for-hydraulic-and-thermal-properties-of-so/)): formula is in table 1 and the example in page 31 uses a bulk density in g/cm3,
2. the source material of the other pedotransfer functions is based on the HYPRES data. In it, bulk density is in Mg/m3, which is the same as g/cm3 (ex : [HYPRESCZ](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Dry-bulk-density-g-cm-3-of-the-samples-stored-in-HYPRESCZ_tbl2_260122387). 
3.  calculation outputs: for Restinclières, the bulk density calculated is around 1.5. If it was in kg/m3, it should be in the thousands. Typical values of bulk densities are between 1.3 and 1.7 g/cm3 [source](https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Typical-values-of-the-bulk-density-for-soil-texture-classes_tbl1_328238567). 

=> All units documented in code should (for both bulkDensity and bulkDensityFineSoil) be changed but also in the excel sheets (pedotransfertBulkDensity). @LECOMTE-ISADEV I changed it in the excel, let me know if you want me to do it in the code as well.

I investigated whether the bulk density was used in code as kg/cm3 or g/cm3, and I think it has not impact. The only time when bulk density was used out of PDF is the following : 
```
if ((this.wiltingPoint/this.bulkDensity) < 0.01)
		this.wiltingPoint = 0.01 * this.bulkDensity;
```
(l. 242 in SafeLayer)
But as the wiltingPoint is in m3/m3, it has no impact.

Virtual experimental design on the influence of pedoclimatic conditions on the LER of agroforestry systems
body: **Objective:** To determine whether soil and climatic conditions influence the efficiency of agroforestry systems, as measured by their LER (Land Equivalent Ratio). **Variables studied:** - Soil depth - Frequency of anoxic conditions (water table depth) **Experimental design**: - Soil depth: from 1 to 10 m in 1 m increments - Frequency of anoxic conditions: groundwater table level from 0 to 10 m in 1 m increments This results in 100 combinations. However, it is actually unnecessary to perform simulations where the water table ceiling is strictly lower than the soil depth, as these would all be identical. For each combination, the three systems : AF, MC, and TF ust be simulated. The standard simulation parameters are used, including two thinning operations and an AF-managed alley that narrows at the 10-year mark.
